summary.one_line: A single-plant, West Bengal-focused flexible-packaging converter whose revenue has more than doubled in two years and whose margins jumped from about 1% to about 10%. But operating cash flow has been negative in every one of those three years, debt and receivables are piling up, related-party dealings are heavy, and there is no visible moat. The IPO mostly funds working capital and debt repayment, not a step-change in the business.
bull_points: Fast growth on paper: revenue from operations rose from Rs 49.53 cr (FY24) to Rs 81.02 cr (FY25) and Rs 115.14 cr (FY26), and PAT rose from Rs 0.64 cr to Rs 4.56 cr and then Rs 10.97 cr (S1).
Operating EBITDA margin widened from 2.60% (FY24) to 9.56% (FY25) and 16.50% (FY26). Q1 FY27 shows 21.76% (S1)(S6).

It is an integrated converter: extrusion, printing, lamination, slitting and pouching under one roof. It holds ISO 9001:2015, ISO 22000:2018 and HACCP certification, which food and dairy packaging needs (S1)(S12).
About 89% of the gross issue is fresh capital (Rs 51.01 cr of Rs 56.68 cr). The OFS is only Rs 5.67 cr, and promoters keep about 70.08% after the issue (S3)(S13).

The company declares nil outstanding litigation by or against itself, its group companies and its KMP. The promoter rows in the summary table are blank rather than marked nil. The only item is one tax proceeding filed by a non-promoter director (S1).
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative in all three years: Rs -3.46 cr, -5.74 cr and -11.46 cr in FY24-FY26, or about Rs -20.7 cr in total against about Rs 16.2 cr of cumulative reported PAT (S1).
Borrowings rose 3.5x in one year, from Rs 13.32 cr (FY25) to Rs 46.82 cr (FY26), and debt/equity was 1.11x at FY26 (S1).
Concentration is extreme: 96.8% of FY26 revenue came from West Bengal, the top 10 customers were 69.44% of sales and the top 10 suppliers were 90.16% of purchases (S11)(S15).
Related-party transactions were 27.63% of FY26 revenue and 40.72% of FY25 revenue. The promoter LLP itself bought about Rs 14.80 cr of goods in FY26 (S10).
An independent SME reviewer called the FY25 onward margin jump something that may 'raise eyebrows' and possibly 'window dressing'. Receivables reached Rs 41.00 cr at June 30, 2026 (S13).
The promoters' own disclosed business experience is short: about 5 years for the MD and about 4 years for the whole-time director (S1).
watch_points: Final category-wise subscription on Nov 4, 2026. Day-1 data was nil or not yet published when this was written (S5)(S18).
Whether anchor allocation was actually made, and to whom. Sources conflict, and no anchor list was found (S14)(S17).
H1 FY27 operating cash flow and receivable days after listing, the single best test of whether the reported margins are real (S1)(S13).
The size and trend of sales to promoter entities, especially Sethsawaria Poly Fab LLP, in the first annual report as a listed company (S10).
Unlock dates: the anchor tranches unlock at 30 and 90 days. Promoter holdings above the 20% minimum unlock in two halves at 1 and 2 years (S20).

reasoning: Reported profits are not converting into cash. Over FY24-FY26 operating cash flow totalled about Rs -20.7 cr while PAT totalled about Rs 16.2 cr, and Q1 FY27 receivables of Rs 41.00 cr exceed the quarter's total income of Rs 30.49 cr. Until cash flow turns positive, the margin expansion from 2.6% to 16.5% EBITDA cannot be taken at face value (S1)(S6)(S13).

The money raised mainly plugs the cash drain rather than building the business. About Rs 24.61 cr goes to working capital and Rs 8.00 cr to debt repayment, against only Rs 6.51 cr for new machinery. The working-capital line was raised from Rs 17.59 cr in the DRHP (S1)(S2)(S13).

There is no visible moat. The company makes commodity LDPE films, laminates and milk and oil pouches in a fragmented market, with 96.8% of revenue in one state, 69.44% from its top 10 customers and orders often taken verbally (S1)(S11)(S15)(S22).

Governance needs more trust than the record supports. A promoter LLP formed in Nov 2023 holds 90% before the IPO, built largely by converting loans and payables into equity. The same LLP is a material customer (about Rs 14.80 cr of FY26 sales), and related-party transactions ran at 27.6% to 40.7% of revenue in FY25-FY26 (S9)(S10).

The promoters disclose only about 4-5 years of business experience, the three independent directors were appointed only in March 2026, and the lead manager's past SME listings are mixed. That is a thin record for a company tripling its debt in a year (S1)(S11)(S13).

subsections.title: What the company makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Vedant Poly Fabs Limited (formerly Vedant Poly Fabs Private Limited, incorporated in 2018) is a business-to-business maker of flexible plastic packaging. Its products are multilayer low-density (LD) films (3-layer and 5-layer), shrink films, barrier films, printed laminates, and milk and oil pouches. Customers use them to package food, beverages and other consumer products (S1). Everything is made to order to the customer's specification of size, thickness, material composition and printing (S15). In practice it is a converter: it turns polymer granules and polyester film into printed, laminated rolls and pouches that a dairy, edible-oil or FMCG packer then fills on its own lines (S7).

The DRHP reports four product segments: Lamination, Printed Plastic, Milk Film and Shrink Film (S1). The mix has changed very quickly. Lamination was 59.22% of FY26 revenue against only 2.44% in FY24 (S11). Manufacturing was 96.37% of FY26 revenue. The remaining 3.63% came from 'bill-to-ship' trading of billets and MS (mild steel) strips, supplied straight from source to customer without holding inventory (S11)(S13). Steel billet trading has nothing to do with packaging. It matters because the promoter LLP's stated activities include iron-ore trading (S9).

The jump in lamination from about 2% to about 59% of revenue in two years coincides with the margin expansion, which suggests (but does not prove) a mix-driven gain. Yet the company says its lamination, slitting and pouching machines were added only in March 2026 (S3)(S7). In FY25 it bought Rs 18.43 cr of goods and Rs 2.12 cr of machinery from a related party, Lakhotia Packwell Pvt Ltd (S10). The public summaries do not explain how laminated product was made or sourced before March 2026. Investors should look for this in the RHP's 'Our Business' chapter.

The company owns and runs a single manufacturing unit at 6/1/Q Digberia Road, Barasat, North 24 Parganas, West Bengal. Lamination, printed flexible laminates, milk film and shrink film are all made there (S1). Installed capacity is reported at 8.85 million kg a year, running at 71.64% utilisation (S11). The process is integrated end to end: raw material buying, film extrusion, printing, lamination, slitting, quality control, packing and dispatch (S2). A reprocessing unit added in March 2026 recycles in-process plastic waste (S2)(S7).

items: Workforce: 72 at March 31, 2026 (41 permanent, 31 contractual), and 61 employees at June 30, 2026, with contract labour hired as needed (S6)(S13).
Logistics: an in-house fleet of 8 vehicles for deliveries (S15).

Sales model: direct sales with an in-house design team and no distributor layer (S8). The DRHP's own risk factors say orders are often received verbally, which can cause order discrepancies and makes scaling harder (S1).
Inputs: LDPE plastic granules, metallocene plastic granules and polyester film. All are petrochemical-linked and their prices move with crude and polymer cycles (S1).
The company claims a 'strategic locational advantage' because the plant is close to some raw-material suppliers, which shortens sourcing times (S1)(S15).

blocks.text: Of the issue money, Rs 6.51 cr goes to plant and machinery at this same Barasat site (S1). One aggregator, summarising the offer document, describes this as an extrusion-coating line and cites a figure of 12.85 million kg (S11). The public sources did not make clear whether that is the new line's capacity or the plant's total after the addition. We could not check it against the RHP itself.

subsections.title: Customers and suppliers: concentration end to end

blocks.text: The customer base is small and concentrated. The DRHP's top-5 customer table (names withheld) shows Customer A at Rs 17.73 cr, B at Rs 14.13 cr, C at Rs 12.54 cr, D at Rs 10.73 cr and E at Rs 6.63 cr (S1). Together that is about Rs 61.76 cr, or 53.64% of FY26 revenue (S12). The top 10 customers were 69.44% of FY26 sales, up from 13.49% in FY24 (S11). So the business has become far more concentrated as it grew.

blocks.caption: Top-5 customers, FY26 (Rs lakh, names withheld in DRHP)

blocks.text: Supply is even more concentrated. The top 5 suppliers provided 79.32% of purchases and the top 10 provided 90.16% (S8)(S11). A related party also sits on the customer side: promoter Sethsawaria Poly Fab LLP bought about Rs 14.80 cr of goods from the company in FY26, roughly 12.9% of revenue (S10). That is close to the size of the top-5 customer slots above, but the DRHP summary does not say whether the LLP is one of the anonymised customers.

One state, one plant, ten customers and ten suppliers carry nearly the whole business. A single lost dairy or edible-oil account, or one supplier disruption, would show up directly in revenue and margins.

The DRHP's industry summary puts the India flexible packaging market at USD 20.41 bn in 2025, forecast to reach USD 35.11 bn by 2030 (11.46% CAGR). It puts the overall India packaging market at USD 101.12 bn in 2025, rising to USD 169.73 bn by 2030 (10.73% CAGR). Globally, flexible packaging is estimated at USD 332.7 bn in 2025, growing at 5.2% a year to 2035 (S1). These are third-party industry figures used in the prospectus. They describe a large, growing pond, not the company's position in it.

blocks.caption: Market data cited in the DRHP

blocks.text: At Rs 115 cr of FY26 revenue, Vedant is a tiny share of the Indian flexible packaging market (S1). Its growth comes from winning share in regional dairy, oil and food packaging in West Bengal, not from the market's growth (S11).

Flexible-packaging converting in India is described as fragmented, with many small and medium enterprises and a few large players with conversion capacity above 5,000 tonnes a year (S22). An experienced SME IPO reviewer also calls Vedant's segment 'highly competitive and fragmented' (S13). The listed peers named in the offer document are B&A Packaging India Ltd and Barflex Polyfilms Ltd (S12). The same reviewer called the peer comparison 'eyewash' because the peers are not truly comparable (S13). Milk-pouch film in particular is a standard LDPE/LLDPE multilayer blown-film product, made by many regional converters across India (S22).

items: No import-substitution claim, market-share claim or 'only Indian maker' claim appears in the DRHP summary. The strengths it lists are generic: integrated manufacturing, quality control, location, product range, in-house logistics, direct sales and workforce (S1).
The ISO 9001, ISO 22000 and HACCP certifications are entry requirements for food-contact packaging, not barriers that competitors cannot clear (S1).
There are no long-term contracts. Orders are often verbal, which suggests customers can switch suppliers easily (S1).
Pricing power looks limited. Reviewers flag that competition may cap pricing and that polymer price swings feed straight into margins (S7).

blocks.text: We see no genuine moat. Vedant is a small regional converter of commodity films and pouches. Its advantages are proximity to customers and suppliers and owner-run service, which any nearby converter can match.

Plastic packaging faces tightening environmental rules in India. Reviewers note that changing plastic-packaging regulations could raise compliance costs (S7)(S12). The company's March 2026 waste-reprocessing unit is a sensible response, but it is in-house scrap recycling, not a structural advantage (S7).

The business also depends on eastern India's demand. The DRHP lists dependence on the eastern region as a top-10 risk factor (S1). With 96.8% of FY26 revenue from West Bengal (S11), any slowdown in the state's dairy and edible-oil packers, or a large competitor entering the region, would hit the company directly.
Industry growth of about 11% a year is a tailwind, but it does not protect a sub-scale player. Larger national converters can underprice it on commodity films.

The DRHP's restated standalone financials show revenue from operations of Rs 49.53 cr (FY24), Rs 81.02 cr (FY25) and Rs 115.14 cr (FY26). That is +63.6% and then +42.1%, or about 52% compounded a year (S1). Profit grew far faster than revenue, from Rs 0.64 cr to Rs 4.56 cr and then Rs 10.97 cr, because operating EBITDA margin expanded from 2.60% to 9.56% and then 16.50% (S1). In Q1 FY27 (the quarter to June 30, 2026) the company reported total income of Rs 30.49 cr and PAT of Rs 3.48 cr, with an EBITDA margin of 21.76% (S6)(S16).

Note: FY24-FY26 figures are from the DRHP abridged prospectus (S1). Q1 FY27 figures are from the RHP-era press release and aggregators (S6)(S16). Some aggregators print FY25 PAT as '4,56,060' (a units error), and one prints FY26 EBITDA as Rs 19.00 cr against the DRHP's Rs 19.18 cr total EBITDA (S2)(S3)(S7). We use the DRHP figures.

A move from 2.6% to 16.5% EBITDA margin in two years, and above 21% in Q1 FY27, is very unusual for a commodity film converter. An independent reviewer said the profit jump from FY25 'raise[s] eyebrows' and that margins look inflated, possibly 'window dressing' (S13). This is not proof of wrongdoing, but the cash-flow data below does not corroborate the profits.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, debt and cash flow

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs lakh)

blocks.text: Operating cash flow was negative in every year shown and got worse as the company grew. Cumulatively it is about Rs -20.7 cr over FY24-FY26, against about Rs 16.2 cr of cumulative PAT (S1). Investing outflows add another Rs 37.8 cr. All of this was funded by financing inflows of Rs 5.85 cr, Rs 12.77 cr and Rs 47.16 cr (S12): fresh borrowing (Rs 46.82 cr by FY26) plus promoter equity (S1). The DRHP itself lists negative operating and investing cash flows as a top-10 risk (S1).

Working capital is the key problem. The working-capital cycle was 160 days in FY26, and net working capital was Rs 46.27 cr (S11). Creditor days collapsed from 167 to 7 (S11). That coincides with related-party payables being converted into equity: in FY25 a purchase-related balance of Rs 7.00 cr owed to the promoter LLP was converted into shares (S10). By June 30, 2026, trade receivables were Rs 41.00 cr, more than the whole quarter's total income of Rs 30.49 cr (S6)(S13). Contingent liabilities were Rs 1.84 cr. Debt/equity was 0.98x at June 30, 2026 (S13).

This is the clearest red flag in the filing: a growing profit line alongside a growing operating cash outflow, rising receivables and a 3.5x rise in debt in one year. Net worth rose from Rs 3.86 cr to Rs 42.26 cr in two years, but most of that came from equity issued against promoter loans and payables, not from retained profit (S1)(S10).

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: The top line is real growth in scale: revenue more than doubled in two years and assets grew about 5x (S1)(S6). But the quality of that growth is weak on three counts. First, it came with much higher customer concentration (top 10 rose from 13.49% to 69.44% of sales) and a near-total focus on one state (S11). Second, profits have not turned into cash in any year (S1). Third, a meaningful slice of revenue involves related parties: 40.72% of revenue in FY25 and 27.63% in FY26 (S10).

items: Supports the story: revenue CAGR of about 52% over FY24-FY26, and capacity utilisation of 71.64% leaves some headroom to grow (S1)(S11).
Undercuts the story: negative CFO in every year, receivables above a quarter's income, and borrowing that rose from Rs 13.32 cr to Rs 46.82 cr (S1)(S13).
Unverifiable from public summaries: whether the FY26 lamination-led margin is repeatable at arm's-length prices (S10)(S11).
No dividends have been paid in the reported periods (S13).

blocks.text: Verdict on financials: the growth is real in volume terms, but its profitability and cash quality are unproven. We would want two half-years of positive operating cash flow before trusting the margins.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.text: This is a book-built SME IPO on NSE Emerge of 60,30,000 equity shares of Rs 10 face value. It is open from Nov 2 to Nov 4, 2026, with allotment on Nov 5 and tentative listing on Nov 9, 2026 (S3)(S13). The task brief says the price band was not yet known, but multiple sources now report a band of Rs 88-94. At the upper end the issue is Rs 56.68 cr (S3)(S4)(S13).

blocks.caption: Issue composition (upper band Rs 94)
rows: Offer for sale (Sethsawaria Poly Fab LLP)

items: Lot size: 1,200 shares. Individual investors must apply for at least 2 lots (2,400 shares), or Rs 2,25,600 at the upper band (S3)(S13).
Pre-issue shares: 1,47,25,214. Post-issue: 2,01,51,614. Promoter and group holding after the issue: 70.08% (S3)(S13).
Lead manager: Affinity Global Capital Market. Registrar: Cameo Corporate Services. Market maker: Giriraj Stock Broking (S3).
In the DRHP the fresh issue was 'up to 54,51,840' shares and the OFS 'up to 6,05,760' shares. The selling LLP's weighted average cost of acquisition was Rs 25.93 per share (S1).

blocks.text: The OFS is small (about 10% of the gross issue), so about 90% of the money stays with the company. That is a positive versus SME issues that are mainly promoter exits.

subsections.title: Objects of the issue: where the fresh money goes

blocks.caption: Use of net fresh-issue proceeds (Rs cr)
rows: Largest use. Raised by Rs 7.02 cr between DRHP and RHP
Against Rs 46.82 cr of debt at FY26
Plant & machinery at existing Barasat unit
Balance of Rs 51.01 cr = GCP + expenses

blocks.text: DRHP figures are from the company's abridged prospectus, dated June 5, 2026 (S1). The Rs 24.61 cr working-capital figure is reported consistently by Chittorgarh, Investorgain and Dilip Davda's review of the offer document (S2)(S6)(S13). Several other aggregators still carry the DRHP's Rs 17.59 cr (S7)(S12)(S14). We could not open the RHP PDF directly (see method). On the RHP numbers, about 48% of the fresh issue funds working capital, about 16% repays debt and only about 13% buys machinery (S2).

The DRHP's own justification for working capital is that the business is 'working capital intensive, requiring funds for trade receivables, inventory, payables, and daily operations' (S1). In plain terms, most of the IPO money refills the cash the business has been consuming. The Rs 8.00 cr repayment cuts debt by only about a sixth (S1).
The objects confirm the cash-flow concern: shareholders' money mainly finances receivables and inventory. Only Rs 6.51 cr goes to new capacity.

The DRHP-era reservation was QIB 50% (with up to 60% of that available to anchors), NII 15% and retail 35% (S8)(S14). Sources for the final category split conflict. Goodreturns shows 17,17,560 shares (28.48%) for anchors and 11,45,040 for QIBs (S17). Chittorgarh's offered-shares table shows only 68,400 QIB shares, 22,60,800 NII and 33,96,000 retail (S3)(S5). We could not reconcile these from available sources.

According to Dilip Davda's review, this is lead manager Affinity Global's 12th mandate in four fiscals. Of its last 11 listings, 4 opened at a discount, 3 at par and the rest at premiums of 5.88% to 51.79%. The reviewer rates that record as average (S13). The same review notes that the offer document reached the public domain only around noon on Oct 30, 2026, with an error in its post-IPO NAV data (S13).
A late document release and a mixed lead-manager record are not disqualifying on their own, but they leave retail investors less time and less assurance.

The promoters are Pankaj Kumar Maheshwari (48), Chairman and Managing Director; Sujata Maheshwari (46), Whole-Time Director; and Sethsawaria Poly Fab LLP (S1). Pankaj holds a B.Com from the University of Burdwan and became a director on March 25, 2021. The DRHP credits him with 'around 5 (Five) years of business experience' because his experience is counted only from his association with this company. Sujata holds a B.Com from Jadavpur University, oversees sales and administration, and has 'approximately 4 (four) years of experience' (S1).

Sethsawaria Poly Fab LLP was formed on Nov 29, 2023, with Pankaj and Sujata as designated partners. Its stated activities are iron-ore trading and dealing in raw materials and finished goods of flexible packaging. The DRHP does not disclose its capital contribution or profit-sharing ratios (S9). The board has six directors: Pankaj, Sujata, Sunil Bihani (Director and CFO) and three independent directors, Ravi Todi, Puja Shaw and Shikha Gupta (S1). The independent directors were appointed on March 27, 2026, shortly before the DRHP was filed (S11).

The disclosed experience is short and has no visible prior packaging track record. The DRHP itself lists the promoters' limited experience with listed companies as a top-10 risk (S1). Weighted average acquisition costs are Rs 17.67 (Pankaj), Rs 12.35 (Sujata) and Rs 20.21 (LLP) per share (S1).

Related-party transactions are not routine here. They totalled Rs 3.89 cr (7.85% of revenue) in FY24, Rs 32.99 cr (40.72%) in FY25 and Rs 31.81 cr (27.63%) in FY26 (S10). The counterparties are promoter or promoter-group entities on both the customer and supplier sides.

blocks.caption: Key related-party transactions (from DRHP, via S10)
rows: Loan taken, then converted to equity
Rs 11 lakh x3, Rs 6 lakh x1
Rs 18.43 cr / Rs 2.12 cr / Rs 1.58 cr

blocks.text: Three points matter. First, the promoter LLP built its 90% stake largely by converting loans and payables into equity (Rs 7.00 cr in FY25 and Rs 15.87 cr in FY26), together with a 50:1 bonus issue in March 2025 (S10)(S11)(S13). Second, the same LLP is also a significant customer, buying about Rs 14.80 cr, or roughly 12.9% of FY26 revenue (S10). That makes arm's-length pricing on those sales central to judging the reported margins. Third, Vedika Laminator Pvt Ltd, a promoter-group entity incorporated on Jan 6, 2026 and owned by the Lakhotias, shares the Lakhotia name with Lakhotia Packwell, the FY25 supplier of goods and machinery (S9)(S10). The public summaries do not spell out how the families are related.

This is not a routine RPT section. A promoter vehicle that is simultaneously the 90% shareholder, a lender converted into equity and a top-tier customer creates real scope for revenue and margin support that outside shareholders cannot verify. The company says the transactions are at arm's length but 'cannot assure' better terms were unavailable from unrelated parties (S10).

The DRHP's litigation summary shows nil criminal, tax, regulatory, SEBI or material civil proceedings by or against the company, its KMP and its group companies. The only item is one tax proceeding initiated by a director who is not a promoter (S1). The promoters are not declared wilful defaulters or fraudulent borrowers and are not debarred by SEBI (S9). The DRHP reports no auditor qualification table in its summary and refers readers to the full document (S1).

items: The company converted from private to public limited in 2025, a typical pre-IPO step (S8).

The DRHP itself contains an inconsistency: it says no loans or advances were given to related parties, yet the FY26 table shows a Rs 23,000 advance to Pankaj Maheshwari (HUF). This is trivial in amount but is a disclosure-quality signal (S10).
The reviewer flagged an error in the offer document's post-IPO NAV data (S13).
No dividend history, and a stated 'prudent dividend policy' (S13).

blocks.text: There is no litigation or regulatory overhang. The governance concerns here come from structure and related-party dealings, not from legal disputes.

items: Cash-flow and earnings quality: three years of negative operating cash flow (cumulative about Rs -20.7 cr), Rs 41.00 cr of receivables at June 2026 and a 160-day working-capital cycle (S1)(S11)(S13).
Leverage: borrowings rose from Rs 13.32 cr to Rs 46.82 cr in FY26. The IPO repays only Rs 8.00 cr (S1).
Related-party dependence: RPTs were 27.63% of FY26 revenue, and the promoter LLP is a roughly Rs 14.80 cr customer (S10).
Customer, geographic and supplier concentration: top 10 customers 69.44%, West Bengal 96.8%, top 10 suppliers 90.16% (S11)(S15).
Single plant at Barasat: any outage, fire or labour dispute halts all production. The DRHP flags manpower and machine intensity as a risk (S1)(S12).
Raw-material price exposure to LDPE granules, metallocene granules and polyester film, with little pricing power in a fragmented market (S1)(S7).
Margin sustainability: an abrupt expansion from 2.6% to 16.5% EBITDA, which independent reviewers questioned (S1)(S13).
SME liquidity: market-maker-driven trading and lot-based dealing make exits hard (S7).

blocks.text: Most of the DRHP's top-10 internal risks are company-specific rather than boilerplate. They include supplier dependence, key-customer dependence, manpower intensity, working-capital needs, verbally received orders, eastern-India concentration, promoters' limited listed-company experience, raw-material prices, receivables and negative cash flows (S1). Taken together they describe a young, cash-hungry, concentrated business.

The cash-flow risk and the related-party risk reinforce each other. If any of the related-party sales are not at arm's-length prices, both the margins and the growth would be overstated, and the negative cash flow would be the symptom.

We could not read the RHP's specific lock-in table. Under the SEBI ICDR framework as amended in 2025, an SME promoter's minimum contribution (20% of post-issue capital) is locked for 3 years. Promoter holdings above that are released in two halves, 50% after 1 year and 50% after 2 years from allotment. Other pre-issue shareholders are locked for 1 year. Anchor shares are locked 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days (S20).

items: Promoters will hold about 70.08% after the issue, so about 50 percentage points of the equity is above the 20% minimum and enters the phased release (S3)(S20).
In practice, roughly 25% of post-issue equity could become sellable by promoters one year after listing, and roughly another 25% after two years (derived from S3 and S20).
IPOWatch lists the anchor lock-in as 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days (S14). One aggregator gives unlock dates of Dec 7, 2026 and Feb 3, 2027, but no confirmed anchor allotment was found (S17).
SEBI has floated a proposal to alter SME lock-ins, including a uniform 1-year lock-in for excess promoter holding. As far as we could find, it was not yet in force for this issue (S21).

blocks.text: SME lock-ins are shorter than the market tends to assume. A large promoter block could become saleable from late 2027.

We found no management interview, analyst call or quoted guidance. The company's pre-IPO press release (distributed by PNN and carried by ANI and ThePrint as an advertorial) contains financial figures and the objects of the issue, but no management quotes or growth targets (S16). The only forward-looking statements come from the DRHP's objects section (S1).

items: On working capital, the company says incremental funds 'will be required in subsequent years to support growth' and are 'expected to enhance operational capacity, improve revenue generation, and support achievement of projected business targets'. The projections themselves are not disclosed in the summary (S1).
On debt, it says repayment will 'reduce our existing borrowings, assist us in maintaining a favorable debt-equity ratio and enable utilization of our internal accruals for further investment' (S1).
On capex, Rs 6.51 cr is for new plant and machinery at the existing Barasat unit (S1). It is described in aggregator coverage as an extrusion-coating line (S11).

blocks.text: Management has not given concrete forward guidance on revenue, margins, new geographies or customers. Any outlook beyond 'more of the same at one plant' is inference, not company statement.

subsections.title: What would need to happen for the story to work

blocks.text: For the IPO to create value, three things must happen. Q1 FY27's margins of 21.76% EBITDA and 11.48% PAT must hold (S6). The new working capital must be followed by positive operating cash flow rather than further receivable build-up (S1)(S13). And the customer base must broaden beyond West Bengal and beyond related parties (S10)(S11). Capacity utilisation of 71.64% implies room for roughly 40% more output from the existing plant before the new line is needed (S11).

The most likely near-term path, on the evidence, is continued top-line growth in the region, funded by IPO cash. The open question is whether it is profitable at arm's-length prices. The first two post-listing half-year results (H1 FY27 and FY27) will be the real test (S1)(S13).
Without disclosed projections or management commentary, investors are effectively buying the extrapolation of a two-year margin surge that has not shown up in cash.

subsections.title: Day-1 status, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: This report was written on Nov 2, 2026, the day the issue opened. As of 08:17 AM on Day 1, IPOGuru showed zero applications in every category, 0x overall, simply because bidding had barely begun (S18). Chittorgarh's subscription page said subscription information was 'not available at this time' (S5). Treat any Day-1 figure as partial. Final numbers come only after the close on Nov 4, 2026.

blocks.caption: Subscription snapshot (Day 1, early; IPOGuru category split, S18)

blocks.text: Anchors: we found no confirmed anchor allotment, amount or investor names. IPOWatch shows the anchor size only as a placeholder (S14), and Goodreturns lists an anchor portion of 17,17,560 shares without names or amounts (S17). The grey market premium (unofficial and unregulated) was reported at Rs 15 on Nov 1-2, 2026 by Investorgain (S6), while IPO Premium listed Rs 0 (S23). These figures conflict and are not an investment signal.

method: Researched on 2026-11-02 (issue opening day). Primary source: the company's Draft Abridged Prospectus, which summarises the DRHP dated June 5, 2026 (S1). It was read page by page and supplied the restated FY24-FY26 financials and KPIs, top-5 customer table, promoter biographies, pre-offer shareholding, DRHP objects, top-10 risk factors and litigation summary. The full RHP was located on the lead manager's site (affinityglobalcap.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RHP.pdf) and on NSE archives (via S19). It could not be read: the PDF exceeded the fetch size limit and direct download was not permitted in this environment. RHP-stage details were therefore cross-verified across at least two secondary sources each: final share counts, the revised Rs 24.61 cr working-capital object, Q1 FY27 figures, capacity and utilisation, customer and supplier concentration, related-party detail, and lead-manager history. The secondary sources were Chittorgarh, Investorgain, IPO Watch/Dilip Davda, Multibagg, 5paisa and Chanakya. Material gaps and conflicts: (1) the working-capital object is Rs 17.59 cr in the DRHP and Rs 24.61 cr in RHP-based sources, and GCP and offer-expense amounts were not found; (2) the final category reservation and anchor allotment conflict across sources, and no anchor names were found; (3) the RHP-specific lock-in table was not read, so lock-ins are stated from the SEBI ICDR framework (S20); (4) the capacity of the proposed line (12.85 mn kg) comes from one aggregator only; (5) Q1 FY27 EBITDA is approximate. Some aggregator errors were ignored: FY25 PAT printed as '4,56,060'; a Multibagg table labelling net worth as total assets; Multibagg 'subscription' figures that are actually reservation percentages; and a Whalesbook article describing the company as a woven-sack maker. Related-party figures come from Multibagg's reading of the DRHP (S10), not from the full RPT note. Valuation metrics (P/E, market-cap-based measures, peer multiples) were deliberately excluded per the brief. GMP is reported only as an unofficial, conflicting data point.
